'''Sir David John Spiegelhalter''' (born 16 August 1953) is a British statistician  and a Fellow of [[Churchill College, Cambridge]].<ref name=googlescholar>{{GoogleScholar|id=oz7MFu0AAAAJ}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.chu.cam.ac.uk/about/fellows/fellows.php |title=Churchill College: Fellows: List of current Fellows |access-date=14 September 2011 |archive-date=18 February 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120218224022/http://www.chu.cam.ac.uk/about/fellows/fellows.php |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=scopus>{{Scopus| id=35491822900}}</ref><ref name=imdb>{{IMDb name|4097227}}</ref> From 2007 to 2018 he was [[Winton Professorship of the Public Understanding of Risk|Winton Professor of the Public Understanding of Risk]] in the [[Faculty of Mathematics, University of Cambridge|Statistical Laboratory]] at the [[University of Cambridge]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~david/ |title=David Spiegelhalter's Personal Home Page |access-date=6 January 2022 |archive-date=7 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210907060836/http://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~david/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Spiegelhalter is an [[ISI highly cited researcher]].

He is currently Chair of the Winton Centre for Risk and Evidence Communication in the [[Centre for Mathematical Sciences (Cambridge)|Centre for Mathematical Sciences]] at Cambridge.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Spiegelhalter|first=D. J.|title=Covid by numbers: making sense of the pandemic with data / David Spiegelhalter and Anthony Masters.|date=2021|others=Anthony Masters|isbn=978-0-241-54773-1|publisher=Pelican|oclc=1250202258}}</ref> On 27 May 2020 he joined the [[UK Statistics Authority#Current board members|board]] of the [[UK Statistics Authority]] as a non-executive director for a period of three years,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/news/appointment-of-two-new-non-executive-directors-to-the-uk-statistics-authority-board/|title=Appointment of two new Non-Executive Directors to the UK Statistics Authority Board|website=Dtatisticsauthoriety.gov.uk|language=en-GB|access-date=27 May 2020}}</ref> a term which was extended through to 2026.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://uksa.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/news/uk-statistics-authority-welcomes-three-new-non-executive-directors/ | title=UK Statistics Authority welcomes three new non-executive directors |website=Uksa.statisticsauthority.gov.uk}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Spiegelhalter was born on 16 August 1953.<ref name="whoswho">{{Who's Who | title=SPIEGELHALTER, Prof. David John | id = U45800 | volume = 2015 | edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]}}</ref> He was educated at [[Barnstaple Grammar School]], a [[State school|state]] grammar school in [[Barnstaple, Devon]], from 1963 to 1970.<ref>{{cite news|first1=Andy|last1=Keeble|title=Barnstaple old boy knighted in Queen's Birthday honours|url=http://www.northdevongazette.co.uk/news/barnstaple-old-boy-knighted-in-queen-s-birthday-honours-1-3647170|newspaper=[[North Devon Gazette]]|date=18 June 2014|archive-date=8 January 2018|access-date=7 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180108062550/http://www.northdevongazette.co.uk/news/barnstaple-old-boy-knighted-in-queen-s-birthday-honours-1-3647170|url-status=dead}}</ref> He then studied mathematics at [[Keble College, Oxford]], graduating with a Bachelor of Arts (BA) degree in 1974.<ref name="WW 2021" /><ref name="cv" /> He moved to [[University College London]], where he gained his Master of Science (MSc) degree in statistics in 1975 and a Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) degree in [[mathematical statistics]] in 1978.<ref name="WW 2021">{{cite web |title=Spiegelhalter, Sir David (John), (born 16 Aug. 1953), Chair, Winton Centre for Risk and Evidence Communication, University of Cambridge, since 2017 (Winton Professor for the Public Understanding of Risk, 2007–18); Fellow, Churchill College, Cambridge |url=http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whoswho/U45800 |website=[[Who's Who 2021]] |publisher=Oxford University Press |access-date=29 August 2021 |language=en |date=1 December 2020}}</ref><ref name="cv" /> His doctoral thesis was titled "Adaptive Inference Using Finite Mixture Models",<ref name="spiegelphd">{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=David|last=Spiegelhalter |title=Adaptive inference using finite mixture models |publisher=University College London |date=1978 |url=http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.473544|author-link= David Spiegelhalter}}</ref> and was [[Doctoral advisor|supervised]] by [[Adrian Smith (statistician)|Adrian Smith]].<ref name="mathgene"/>

==Career==
Spiegelhalter was research assistant in [[Brunel University]] in 1976<ref name =cv>{{cite web |title=CURRICULUM VITAE – David John SPIEGELHALTER |url=https://understandinguncertainty.org/files/cv-DJS-full.pdf |website=Understanding Uncertainty |access-date=10 May 2019}}</ref> and then visiting lecturer at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], 1977–78. After his PhD, he was a research assistant for the [[Royal College of Physicians]]; he was based at the [[University of Nottingham]], where his PhD supervisor, [[Adrian Smith (statistician)|Adrian Smith]], had been appointed a professor.{{citation needed|date=December 2022}}

From 1981 he was at the Medical Research Council Biostatistics Unit at Cambridge. He has been an honorary lecturer at the [[University of Hong Kong]] since 1991. He has also been a consultant for [[GlaxoSmithKline]], [[Novartis]] and the [[World Anti-Doping Agency]]. He played a leading role in the [[List of public inquiries in the United Kingdom|public inquiries]] into children's heart surgery at the [[Bristol Royal Infirmary]], the murders by [[Harold Shipman]],<ref>{{cite news| url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/programmes/panorama/4868560.stm | work=BBC News | title=Programme transcript | date=2 April 2006}}</ref> the independent inquiry on [[Mid Staffordshire NHS Foundation Trust|Mid Staffs Trust]] and, more recently, the [[Infected Blood Inquiry|infected blood]] inquiry.

Between 2007 and 2012 he divided his work<ref>{{cite book|title=CAM|publisher=Cambridge University Alumni Association|issue=58|date=October 2009|chapter-url=http://www.alumni.cam.ac.uk/sites/www.alumni.cam.ac.uk/files/documents/CAM58.pdf#page=5|page=3|chapter=Don's Diary|first=David|last=Spiegelhalter|access-date=21 October 2014|archive-date=3 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303232446/http://www.alumni.cam.ac.uk/sites/www.alumni.cam.ac.uk/files/documents/CAM58.pdf#page=5|url-status=dead}}</ref> between the Cambridge [[Statistical Laboratory, University of Cambridge|Statistical Laboratory]] (three-fifths) and the [[Medical Research Council (UK)|Medical Research Council]] [[Biostatistics]] Unit (two-fifths).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/About%20Us/People.html |title=MRC Biostatistics Unit: People |access-date=15 September 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110903103326/http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/About%20Us/People.html |archive-date=3 September 2011 }}</ref> He left the MRC in March 2012<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/People/formerstaff.html |title=Welcome to the MRC Biostatistics Unit |access-date=25 April 2012 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120113232213/http://www.mrc-bsu.cam.ac.uk/People/formerstaff.html |archive-date=13 January 2012 }}</ref> and worked full-time at the Statistical Laboratory as the [[Winton Professorship of the Public Understanding of Risk|Winton Professor of the Public Understanding of Risk]] until his retirement. He remained chair of the Winton Centre until it closed in 2023. As of 2012 Spiegelhalter has supervised 7 PhD students.<ref name =cv/><ref>{{cite web |title=David John Spiegelhalter |url=https://genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=62175 |website=Mathematics Genealogy Project |access-date=2 September 2019}}</ref>

[[File:David_crop.jpg|thumb|David Spiegelhalter playing with Arco Iris [[Samba band]], July 2009]]

In 2012, Spiegelhalter hosted the [[BBC Four]] documentary ''Tails You Win: The Science of Chance'' which described the application of [[probability]] in everyday life.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/p00yh2rc|title=BBC Four - Tails You Win: The Science of Chance|website=BBC|access-date=13 August 2026}}</ref> He also presented a 2013 [[Cambridge Science Festival]] talk, ''How to Spot a Shabby Statistic'' at the Babbage Lecture Theatre in Cambridge.<ref name=imdb/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.festival.cam.ac.uk/|title=Cambridge Festival|website=Festival.cam.ac.uk|access-date=13 August 2026}}</ref>

He was elected as President of the [[Royal Statistical Society]], and took up the position on 1 January 2017. His Presidential address later that year took as its subject ''Trust in Numbers''.<ref>{{cite journal|year=2017|volume=180|title=Trust in numbers|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A|author=Spiegelhalter, D.|issue=4 |pages=949–965|doi=10.1111/rssa.12302}}</ref>

In March 2020 Spiegelhalter launched a podcast called ''Risky Talk'' where he interviews experts in risk and evidence communication on topics like genetics, nutrition, climate change and immigration.<ref>[https://riskytalk.libsyn.com/ ''Risky Talk'' website]. Accessed 30 December 2022.</ref> He appeared on [[Desert Island Discs|BBC Desert Island Discs]] on 6 February 2022.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Desert Island Discs – Professor Sir David Spiegelhalter, statistician – BBC Sounds|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sounds/play/m0014644|access-date=11 February 2022|website=www.bbc.co.uk|language=en-GB}}</ref>

==Research==
Spiegelhalter's research interests are in statistics<ref name=googlescholar/><ref name="dblp">{{DBLP|name=David J. Spiegelhalter}}</ref> including
* [[Bayesian statistics|Bayesian]] approach to clinical trials, expert systems and complex modelling and epidemiology.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Spiegelhalter | first1 = D. J. | last2 = Best | first2 = N. G.|author2-link= Nicky Best | last3 = Carlin | first3 = B. P. | last4 = Linde | first4 = A. V. D. | title = Bayesian Measures of Model Complexity and Fit | journal = Journal of the Royal Statistical Society | volume = 64 | issue = 4 | doi = 10.1111/1467-9868.00353 | pages = 583–639 | year = 2002 | doi-access = free }}</ref>
*[[Graphical model]]s of conditional independence. He wrote several papers in the 1980s that showed how probability could be incorporated into expert systems, a problem that seemed intractable at the time. Spiegelhalter showed that while [[frequentist]] probability did not lend itself to expert systems, [[Bayesian probability]] most certainly did.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Lauritzen | first1 = S. L. | last2 = Spiegelhalter | first2 = D. J. | title = Local Computations with Probabilities on Graphical Structures and Their Application to Expert Systems | journal = Journal of the Royal Statistical Society | volume = 50 | issue = 2 | pages = 157–224 | jstor = 2345762| year = 1988 | doi = 10.1111/j.2517-6161.1988.tb01721.x }}</ref>
*[[Statistical software]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Markov Chain Monte Carlo in Practice |first1=W. R. |last1=Gilks |first2=S. |last2=Richardson |first3=D. J. |last3=Spiegelhalter |publisher=Chapman & Hall |year=1996 |isbn=978-0-412-05551-5}}</ref> In the 1990s Spiegelhalter led the [[Medical Research Council (UK)|Medical Research Council]] team that developed [[WinBUGS|WinBUGS ("Bayesian analysis Using Gibbs Sampling")]], a statistical-modelling system allowing [[hierarchical Bayes model|hierarchical]] [[prior distribution]]s. WinBUGS and its successor [[OpenBUGS]] specifies [[graphical model]]s using acyclic directed graphs whose nodes are random variables, which are updated using [[Gibbs sampling]] (an updating method for [[Markov chain Monte Carlo]] (MCMC) [[simulation]]).<ref name="WinBUGS">{{Cite journal | last1 = Lunn | first1 = D. | last2 = Spiegelhalter | first2 = D. | last3 = Thomas | first3 = A. | last4 = Best | first4 = N. | title = The BUGS project: Evolution, critique and future directions | journal = Statistics in Medicine | volume = 28 | issue = 25 | pages = 3049–3067 | year = 2009 | doi = 10.1002/sim.3680|doi-access=free| pmid=19630097}}</ref> Earlier Bayesian software had required that the probability distribution for the observed data be an [[exponential family]] and that the prior be its [[Conjugate prior|conjugate distribution]]. Allowing flexible choices of prior distributions simplified hierarchical modelling and helped to promote [[multilevel model]]s, which became widely used in epidemiology and education.
*General issues in [[clinical trials]],<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Neuenschwander | first1 = B. | last2 = Capkun-Niggli | first2 = G. | last3 = Branson | first3 = M. | last4 = Spiegelhalter | first4 = D. J. | title = Summarizing historical information on controls in clinical trials | doi = 10.1177/1740774509356002 | journal = Clinical Trials | volume = 7 | issue = 1 | pages = 5–18 | year = 2010 | pmid =  20156954| s2cid = 38751711 }}</ref> including cluster randomisation, meta-analysis and ethical monitoring.
*Monitoring and comparing clinical and public-health outcomes and their associated publication as performance indicators.
*Public understanding of risk,<ref>{{Cite journal
| last1 = Spiegelhalter | first1 = D.
| last2 = Pearson | first2 = M.
| last3 = Short | first3 = I.
| doi = 10.1126/science.1191181
| title = Visualizing Uncertainty About the Future
| journal = Science
| volume = 333
| issue = 6048
| pages = 1393–1400
| year = 2011
| pmid = 21903802
| bibcode = 2011Sci...333.1393S
| citeseerx = 10.1.1.1029.4615
| s2cid = 1223740
}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://understandinguncertainty.org/blogs/david |title=David Spiegelhalter's blog &#124; Understanding Uncertainty |access-date=15 September 2011}}</ref> including promoting concepts such as the [[micromort]] (a one in a million chance of death) and [[microlife]] (a 30-minute reduction of life expectancy). Media reporting of statistics,<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Riesch | first1 = H. | last2 = Spiegelhalter | first2 = D. J. | doi = 10.1080/13698575.2010.540645 | title = 'Careless pork costs lives': Risk stories from science to press release to media | journal = Health, Risk & Society | volume = 13 | pages = 47–64 | year = 2011 | s2cid = 72065012 }}</ref> risk and probability and the wider conception of uncertainty as going beyond what is measured to model uncertainty, the unknown and the unmeasurable.

In 2003 Spiegelhalter and others published a paper on the many murders of physician [[Harold Shipman]], in which they found that routine statistical monitoring of mortality could have revealed the murders in 1996, two years and many murders before suspicions were actually raised.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Spiegelhalter | first1=David|last2=Grigg|first2=Olivia|last3=Kinsman|first3=Robin|last4=Treasure|first4=Tom | title=Risk-adjusted sequential probability ratio tests: applications to Bristol, Shipman and adult cardiac surgery | journal=International Journal for Quality in Health Care | volume=15 | issue=1 | date=1 February 2003 | doi=10.1093/intqhc/15.1.7| pages=7–13 | url=https://academic.oup.com/intqhc/article-pdf/15/1/7/5086350/150007.pdf}}</ref>
